documentNotes.title: General note
documentNotes.statement:
**General note.** Maybe not all problems have correct questions. Some questions (maybe the main question of the problem, maybe one of the subquestions) may make no real sense. In this case you have to write in your answer (in English or Russian): «**impossible situation – ситуация невозможна**». Of course, this answer has to be explained numerically or logically.

**Data from the tables** (Planetary data, stars, constants, etc.) may be used for solving every problem.

The answers «**Да-Yes**» or «**Нет-No**» have to be written in English or Russian.

problems.title: RadioAstron
problems.statement: The RadioAstron project is an international collaborative mission lead by Astro-Space Center of Russian Academy of Sciences. On July 18, 2011 a satellite, «Spektr-R», carrying a 10-m (in diameter) space radio-telescope was launched into an elliptical orbit around the Earth. Together with Earth-based radio-telescopes, «Spektr-R» works as interferometer. RadioAstron operates at the standard radio astronomical wavelengths of 1.19–1.63 cm (K-band), 6.2 cm (C-band), 18 cm (L-band), and 92 cm (P-band). Now «Spektr-R» is rotating in a very elongated orbit with a period $\tau = 8.3$ days and a height of perigee h = 600 km from the Earth surface.

parts.statement: Estimate the maximum resolving power (angular resolution in arcsec) of RadioAstron. Draw a schematic picture, explaining your choice of the situation when it may occur.
Estimate the resolving power of RadioAstron if the target is observed in the direction of the major axis of «Spektr-R» orbit, and also draw a schematic picture.

solution.statement: Official English solution sketch. The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: Resolution and base
sections.statement:
The resolution of the instrument is determined by the working wavelength $\lambda$, and the base $D$. For telescopes the base is just the diameter of the front lens or mirrors, and for interferometers it is the distance between its elements, or, rather, the projection of this distance on the plane perpendicular to the direction to the object under research.

$$\delta=\lambda/D.$$

Thus, the maximum resolution is achieved in the case of the minimum wavelength and the maximum base.

$$\delta_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}/D_{\max}.$$

sections.title: 1.1. Maximum resolving power
sections.statement:
In our case it is achieved at the wavelength $\lambda_{\min}=1.2\ \mathrm{cm}$ and the base of the Earth–“Spektr-R”, in which “Spektr-R” is at apogee, and the ground-based telescope is at the opposite side of the globe; and while the observations are held in the directions perpendicular to the base of Earth–“Spektr-R”, that is perpendicular to the major axis of the orbit:

$$D_{\max}=A+R,$$

where A is the distance at apogee, and R is radius of the Earth. The apogee distance can be found as

$$A=2a-(R+h),$$

where a is semi-major axis of the orbit, which, in turn, follows Kepler’s third law. Comparing the motion of the satellite with the motion of the Moon we get:

$$a^3/a_{\mathrm{Moon}}^3=\tau^2/T_{\mathrm{Moon}}^2;\qquad a=a_{\mathrm{Moon}}(\tau/T_{\mathrm{Moon}})^{2/3},$$

$$a=384\,400\ \mathrm{km}\times(8.3\ \mathrm{days}/27.32\ \mathrm{days})^{2/3}=173\,700\ \mathrm{km}.$$

$$D_{\max}=2a-(R+h)+R=2a-h,$$

$$D_{\max}=2\times173\,700\ \mathrm{km}-600\ \mathrm{km}\approx347\,000\ \mathrm{km}.$$

$$\delta_{\min}=1.2\ \mathrm{cm}/347\,000\ \mathrm{km}\approx3.5\cdot10^{-11}\ \mathrm{rad},$$

or in angular seconds:

$$\delta_{\min}=3.5\cdot10^{-11}\ \mathrm{rad}\times206265^{\prime\prime}/\mathrm{rad}\approx7\cdot10^{-6}\,{}^{\prime\prime}=7\ \mu\mathrm{as}.$$

![Orbit and maximum interferometer base perpendicular to the major axis](#p1-orbit-major-astra-s4-r1)

figures.alt: Orbit and maximum interferometer base perpendicular to the major axis

sections.title: 1.2. Observation along the major axis
sections.statement:
In observations of objects located in the direction of the major axis of the orbit of “Spektr-R” the maximum base D will be equal to the sum of the semi-minor axis of the orbit and the radius of Earth:

$$D_{\max}=b+R.$$

Semi-minor axis can be found from the geometric properties of the ellipse:

$$a^2=b^2+(a-P)^2,\qquad b^2=[a^2-(a-P)^2]^{1/2},$$

$$b\approx48\,900\ \mathrm{km}.$$

$$D_{\max}=48\,900\ \mathrm{km}+6\,400\ \mathrm{km}=55\,300\ \mathrm{km}.$$

$$\delta_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}/D_{\max}=1.2\ \mathrm{cm}/55\,300\ \mathrm{km}\approx2.2\cdot10^{-10}\ \mathrm{rad},$$

or in angular seconds:

$$\delta_{\min}=2.2\cdot10^{-11}\ \mathrm{rad}\times206265^{\prime\prime}/\mathrm{rad}\approx4.5\cdot10^{-5}\,{}^{\prime\prime}=45\ \mu\mathrm{as}.$$

*Source note: the key prints $b^2$ on the left of the square-root formula, and $10^{-11}$ in the final angular conversion after $10^{-10}$ in the preceding line. These printed discrepancies are retained; its stated result is 45 μas.*

![Semi-minor axis and interferometer base for observation along the major axis](#p1-orbit-minor-astra-s4-r1)

figures.alt: Semi-minor axis and interferometer base for observation along the major axis

sections.statement:

- General approach, formula $\delta=\lambda/D$ — 0.5 pt.
- The base for interferometers it is the distance between its elements — 0.5 pt.
- Understanding $\delta_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}/D_{\max}$ — 0.5 pt.

**1.1. Totally 3.5 pt, including:**

- The maximum base of the Earth–“Spektr-R”, in which “Spektr-R” is at apogee, and the ground-based telescope is at the opposite side of the globe $D_{\max}=A+R$ — 0.5 pt.
- The directions perpendicular to the base of Earth–“Spektr-R” — perpendicular to the major axis — 0.5 pt.
- The apogee distance can be found as $A=2a-(R+h)$ — 0.5 pt.
- Using Kepler’s third law to find a, $a^3/a_{\mathrm{Moon}}^3=\tau^2/T_{\mathrm{Moon}}^2$ — 0.5 pt.
- Final calculations and correct result — 1 pt.

**1.2. Totally 3 pt, including:**

- The maximum base $D_{\max}=b+R$ — 1 pt.
- Calculation semi-minor axis using the geometric properties of the ellipse — 1 pt.
- Final calculations and correct result — 1 pt.

problems.title: Gliese 581 g
problems.statement: This celestial body in the system of the star Gliese 581 is the most Earth-like planet found outside the Solar System, and the exoplanet with the greatest recognized potential for harboring albuminous based life.

parts.statement: Estimate orbital period $\tau$ of Gliese 581 g. Consider the orbit to be circular.

Assume intelligent life resides on Gliese 581 g. The civilization uses radio-waves. Is it possible to determine the size (diameter) of the planet by observations on RadioAstron (**«да-yes»** or **«нет-no»**)? Justify the answer by calculations.

solution.statement: Official English solution sketch. The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: 2.1. Orbital period
sections.statement:
It is obvious that there should be about the same conditions as on the Earth for the existence of albuminous based life on the planet.

(Following in the solution indexes G refer to the system Gliese 581, and indexes $\odot$ and E — to the Sun and Earth).

In the “data of some stars” table one can find the mass of the star Gliese 581, which is equal to $\mathcal M_G=0.31\mathcal M_{\odot}$, its parallax $p=0.16^{\prime\prime}$, and the apparent bolometric magnitude $m=8^{\mathrm m}.0$.

Knowing the parallax and the apparent bolometric magnitude of the star, one can find its absolute bolometric magnitude:

$$M=m+5^{\mathrm m}+5^{\mathrm m}\lg p=8^{\mathrm m}.0+5^{\mathrm m}+(-3^{\mathrm m}.98)\approx9^{\mathrm m}.0.$$

It is $9^{\mathrm m}-4^{\mathrm m}.8=4^{\mathrm m}.2$ greater than the absolute magnitude of the Sun. Thus, the radiation from Gliese 581 is $I_{\odot}/I_G=10^{4.2/2.5}\approx48$ times less than that of the Sun.

Taking into account the Stefan–Boltzmann law, let us compare the temperature regimes on Earth ($T_E$) and on the planet Gliese 581 g ($T_G$).

It is known that the balance temperature T on the planet is defined by the balance of incoming and radiated energy. The radiated energy depends only on the surface area and the temperature (the dependence on the temperature is described by the Stefan–Boltzmann law $E\sim T^4$, but it is not necessary to know the exact relationship for the task). In absence of internal sources of energy (we make this assumption) the radiated energy is equal to the energy coming from the central luminary. Both the radiated and incoming energies are proportional to the surface area of the planet, hence the balance does not depend on the size of the planet. The incoming energy is proportional to the radiation of the central star and inversely proportional to the distance to the star:

$$E_E\sim I_{\odot}/R_E^2,\qquad E_G\sim I_G/R_G^2.$$

Thus, for the temperatures on Earth and Gliese 581 g to be equal, it is necessary that

$$E_E=E_G\quad\text{or}\quad R_G/R_E=(I_G/I_{\odot})^{1/2}.$$

According to the generalized Kepler’s third law

$$\tau^2\mathcal M/a^3=\mathrm{const},\quad\text{that is}\quad\tau\sim a^{3/2}/\mathcal M^{1/2},$$

or as the orbits are circular,

$$\tau\sim R^{3/2}/\mathcal M^{1/2},\qquad\tau_G/\tau_E=(R_G/R_E)^{3/2}/(\mathcal M_G/\mathcal M_{\odot})^{1/2},$$

$$\tau_G=\tau_E(R_G/R_E)^{3/2}/(\mathcal M_G/\mathcal M_{\odot})^{1/2}=\tau_E(I_G/I_{\odot})^{3/4}/(\mathcal M_G/\mathcal M_{\odot})^{1/2},$$

$$\tau_G=365\ \mathrm{days}\times48^{-3/4}/0.31^{1/2},\qquad\tau_G\approx36\ \mathrm{days}.$$

sections.title: 2.2. Determining the diameter
sections.statement:
The size of the planet could be determined by recording the radio-sources from different points of the planet’s surface (result of an activity of the civilization). In order to get at least some estimate of the size of the planet, one needs to get a “picture” of radio-sources distribution, and the angular size of the “picture” should exceed the angular resolution at least several times. It should be assumed that as the planet Gliese 581 g is similar to Earth, its diameter is comparable to the diameter of Earth $D_E$, at least in an order of the value. The angular size of a body with a diameter of Earth $D_E$ in system of Gliese 581 is equal to

$$\alpha=p\times D_E/R_E,$$

$$\alpha=0.16^{\prime\prime}\times12.8\ \text{thous km}/149\,600\ \text{thous km}\approx14\cdot10^{-6}\,{}^{\prime\prime}=14\ \mu\mathrm{as}.$$

As we see, this value is comparable with the best angular resolution of RadioAstron, and for the most of positions of the “Spektr-R” it is even less. In order to obtain any reasonable result an “image” have to be taken, that is the angular size of the object have to exceed the angular resolution at least several times. It is not possible to get a “picture”, only a spot will appear as evidence of the extended radio-source. Thus only, it is clear that radio-sources are not at one point but at different locations. In the best case it will be able to determine the order of the diameter of the planet (which we had known earlier).

Answer: «нет-no».

*Note. The size of the planet Gliese 581 g, determined by other methods, is estimated as $1.4\pm0.2$ of the size of Earth. The ratio of 1.4 does not introduce considerable amendments to the solution.*

sections.title: Official basic criteria
sections.statement:
**2.1. Totally 5.5 pt, including:**

- Conditions as on the Earth, the same temperature — 0.5 pt.
- Correct taking the necessary data from the tables — 0.5 pt.
- Finding (any way) that the radiation from Gliese 581 is about 48 times less than that of the Sun — 1.5 pt.
- Dependence on R — 0.5 pt.
- Correct using the generalized Kepler’s third law, calculations — 1.5 pt.
- Final calculations and correct result — 1 pt.

**2.2. Totally 2.5 pt, including:**

- Issue that the order of the size of the planet is comparable to the size of Earth — 0.5 pt.
- $\alpha=p\times D_E/R_E$ — 0.5 pt.
- Correct calculations, result about 14 μas — 0.5 pt.
- Conclusion that the angular size of the object has to exceed the angular resolution at least several times, answer “no” — 1 pt.

Reference diagram supplied for group β:

parts.statement: What is the apparent magnitude of our Sun and
what is the approximate constellation in which our Sun will be seen when observed from the planet Gliese 581 g?
Estimate the angular diameter of the star Gliese 581 when observed from the planet Gliese 581 g.

solution.statement: Official English solution sketch. The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: 3.1. Apparent magnitude
sections.statement:
The magnitude of the Sun, visible from any remote location is

$$m_{\odot}=m_0+5^{\mathrm m}\log(206265)-5^{\mathrm m}\lg p,$$

where $m_0$ is the apparent magnitude of the Sun visible from Earth, and p is the annual parallax of the location.

The magnitude of the Sun as seen from the system of Gliese 581 is

$$m_{\odot}=-26^{\mathrm m}.74+26^{\mathrm m}.57-5^{\mathrm m}\log0.16=-0^{\mathrm m}.17-(-3^{\mathrm m}.98)\approx3^{\mathrm m}.8.$$

(And it is not the only way of solution. The value can be found in many other ways, e.g., by formula $m_{\odot}=M-5^{\mathrm m}+5^{\mathrm m}\lg p$).

*Source note: the double minus in the intermediate expression is written here as $-0^{\mathrm m}.17-(-3^{\mathrm m}.98)$ with parentheses for readability; the alternative formula above is retained as printed, including its plus sign before $5\lg p$.*

sections.title: 3.2. Approximate constellation
sections.statement:
While observing from the planet Gliese 581 g, our Sun will be at point opposite where the system of Gliese 581 is seen from Earth. Because Gliese 581 is located in the zodiacal constellation of Libra, the sun will be approximately in the opposite zodiacal constellation, that is, in the constellation of Aries. (That solution is correct enough.)

*Note: Using a sky-chart one can solve the problem more accurately. The point opposite to the location of the system Gliese 581 at the Earth’s sky, has the coordinates $03^{\mathrm h}\ 19^{\mathrm m}\ 27^{\mathrm s}$ and $07^\circ43^{\prime}20^{\prime\prime}$. This point is located in the constellation of Taurus (Tau), very close to the borders of the constellations of Cetus (Cet) and Aries (Ari). As the students were not provided by a sky-chart, and the question was “what is the approximate constellation”, the answer “approximately in the constellation, opposite to the constellation of Libra, that is in the constellation of Aries” is correct.*

sections.title: 3.3. Angular diameter
sections.statement:
To keep the heat balance a Gliese 581 g should receive the same amount of energy per unit area as is received at Earth.

(As in the previous solution G indices refer to the system of Gliese 581, and indices $\odot$ and E — to the Sun and the Earth).

From the given tables one may find that the spectral class of the star Gliese 581 is M3V. According to the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram the temperature of the star, corresponding to this spectral class, is about $T_G=3300\ \mathrm K$. It is $T_{\odot}/T_G=5780/3300\approx1.75$ times less than the temperature of the Sun.

According to the Stefan–Boltzmann law the power emitted from the star is $P=\sigma\cdot ST^4$, and in just the same way we can discourse about the apparent angular area from which the radiation is coming.

Thus, since the apparent angular area of a star is proportional to the square of its apparent angular diameter, the following equations should be correct:

$$\frac\pi4\alpha_G^2T_G^4=\frac\pi4\alpha_{\odot}^2T_{\odot}^4\quad\text{or}\quad\alpha_G=\alpha_{\odot}(T_{\odot}/T_G)^2,$$

$$\alpha_G=32^{\prime}\cdot(1.75)^2=98^{\prime}.$$

More than three times larger than the Sun!

sections.title: Official basic criteria
sections.statement:
**3.1. Totally 3.5 pt, including:**

- Formulae for magnitude of the Sun (any way solution) — 2 pt.
- Correct calculations — 1.5 pt.

**3.2. Totally 2 pt, including:**

- Understanding that Gliese 581 is located in the zodiacal constellation of Libra — 0.5 pt.
- Sun will be at opposite point — 1 pt.
- Answer: constellation of Aries — 0.5 pt.

**3.3. Totally 2.5 pt, including:**

- Heat balance, the same amount of energy per unit area — 0.5 pt.
- Finding spectral class and temperature (using HR diagram) — 0.5 pt.
- Using Stefan–Boltzmann law — 0.5 pt.
- Final formula — 0.5 pt.
- Final calculations and result — 0.5 pt.

problems.title: XVIII century. Midday.
problems.statement:
(Dubingiai is the nearest town to the accommodation place of XVIII IAO.).

There were different systems of units of measurement in the history of science. This problem is to use historical (at present obsolete) units of measurement.

**Units of power**

1 horse-power (hp) = 735.49875 W.

**Local units of length in the end of XVIII century**

- 1 arshin (arsh) = 0.711187 m
- 1 span (sp) = 1/4 arshin
- 1 vershok (vrsh) = 1/4 span
- 1 sajene (sj) = 3 arshin
- 1 verst (vrst) = 500 sajene

![Map of Lithuania with geographic coordinates and towns](#p4-lithuania-astra-s4-r1)

figures.alt: Photograph: a light-coloured horse with a dark mane standing on grass, held by a woman in Lithuanian folk costume on the right.
Map of Lithuania with geographic coordinates and towns

parts.statement:
Calculate the capacity of the solar energy that in the end of the XVIII century fell on the unit of area of the territory in the outskirts of Dubingiai at midday time:

in winter, in spring, in autumn, and in summer.

The answer must be given using only the «new» physical units, which were coming into operation in those days in this area: horse-powers per square verst.

![Photograph: a light-coloured horse with a dark mane standing on grass, held by a woman in Lithuanian folk costume on the right.](#p4-fig1-astra-s4-r1)

Estimate also the capacity of the solar energy incident on a local horse those times. The answer must also be expressed in physical units, which were coming into operation in those days. What can be surprising about the right answer?

solution.statement: Official English solution sketch. The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: Solar constant in historical units
sections.statement:
Horse-powers per square verst is a power per unit of area, the quantity that dimension is similar to the solar constant. In physics, it is properly called the “power flux”.

Let us calculate the solar constant in units, which were coming into operation in the end of the XVIII century.

**I method — visual.**

The energy-release of the Sun has not changed since the end of the XVIII century and in units of the horse-power is

$$L=3.86\cdot10^{26}\ \mathrm W/(735.5\ \mathrm{W/hp})=5.25\cdot10^{23}\ \text{horse-powers}.$$

The distance from the Sun to Earth has not changed since the end of the XVIII century as well, and in versts is

$$a=1\ \mathrm{AU}=1.496\cdot10^{11}\ \mathrm m/(3\cdot500\cdot0.7112\ \mathrm{m/vrst})=1.402\cdot10^8\ \mathrm{vrst}.$$

Thus, the solar constant in units of the end of the XVIII century is

$$A_{\mathrm{XIX}}=L/(4\pi a^2)=\frac{5.25\cdot10^{23}\ \mathrm{hp}}{4\pi(1.402\cdot10^8\ \mathrm{vrst})^2}=2.12\cdot10^6\ \mathrm{hp/vrst^2}.$$

**II method — formal.**

$$A_{\mathrm{XIX}}=A_0\,k_{(\mathrm{hp/W})}/k_{(\mathrm{vrst/m})}^{2}=\frac{1367\ \mathrm{W/m^2}}{735.5\ \mathrm{W/hp}}(1066.78\ \mathrm{m/vrst})^2=2.12\cdot10^6\ \mathrm{hp/vrst^2}.$$

*Source note: the key’s subscript “XIX” is retained although the problem concerns the XVIII century.*

sections.title: 4.1. Midday power flux
sections.statement:
The outskirts of Dubingiai in the XVIII century were located on the same latitude as where they are located in the XXI century, that is, at about latitudes 54.7°–55.2° (latitudes of Vilnius and Moletai respectively, may be found from the map). The value of 23.5°, the inclination of the equatorial plane of the ecliptics, also almost has not changed (strictly speaking, it had declined by about one minute). Thus, at the middays of the winter solstice in the XVIII century in the outskirts of the town Dubingiai the sun was at an altitude about

$$h_W=90^\circ-55.0^\circ-23.5^\circ=11.5^\circ,$$

at the middays of spring and autumn — at an altitude about

$$h_0=90^\circ-55.0^\circ=35.0^\circ,$$

at the middays of the summer solstice — at an altitude about

$$h_S=90^\circ-55.0^\circ+23.5^\circ=58.5^\circ.$$

While the altitude of the Sun is h, the power flux to the unit of the territory is

$$W=A\sin h.$$

Thus, the target values are:

- in winter — $W_W=A\sin h_W\approx420\,000\ \mathrm{hp/vrst^2}$;
- in spring and autumn — $W_0=A\sin h_0\approx1\,220\,000\ \mathrm{hp/vrst^2}$;
- in summer — $W_S=A\sin h_S\approx1\,810\,000\ \mathrm{hp/vrst^2}$.

sections.title: 4.2. Solar power incident on a horse
sections.statement:
And what is the capacity of the solar energy incident at those times on a local horse? This value largely depends on the orientation of the horse relative to the Sun than the altitude of the sun above the horizon. Let us assume that the cross-sectional area of a horse perpendicular to the sun-rays is 1–3 arsh² (depending on the mentioned above orientation of the horse) and recalculate the value of the solar constant into horse-powers per square arshin.

Distance from the Sun

$$a=1\ \mathrm{AU}=1.496\cdot10^{11}\ \mathrm m/(0.7112\ \mathrm{m/arsh})=2.103\cdot10^{14}\ \mathrm{arsh}.$$

The solar constant in these units equals to

$$A=L/(4\pi a^2)=\frac{5.25\cdot10^{23}\ \mathrm{hp}}{4\pi(2.103\cdot10^{11}\ \mathrm{arsh})^2}=0.94\ \mathrm{hp/arsh^2}.$$

Thus, a horse standing in the sun, receives about one to three horse-powers of solar radiation! Just this can be a surprise.

Answer: 1–3 hp.

*Note. In solving the problem we emphasize very often that many of the physical parameters are not changed in the last two centuries: the solar constant, the distance from Earth to the Sun, the latitude of location, inclination of the ecliptic to the equatorial plane. Students who also record this constancy, should be encouraged to add points.*

*Source note: the distance conversion prints $2.103\cdot10^{14}$ arsh, but the following formula uses $2.103\cdot10^{11}$ arsh. Both printed exponents are retained.*

sections.title: Official basic criteria
sections.statement:
**4.common. Totally 2 pt, including:**

- Calculation of the solar constant in necessary units, result $2.12\cdot10^6$ hp/vrst² or 0.94 hp/arsh² — 2 pt.

**4.1. Totally 3 pt, including:**

- Latitudes the same as now (about 54.7°–55.2°) — 1 pt.
- Calculation of altitudes of midday Sun in winter, spring, autumn, summer — 1 pt.
- $W=A\sin h$, correct final calculations — 1 pt.

**4.2. Totally 3 pt, including:**

- Correct understanding on what the answer may depend — 0.5 pt.
- Correct model of horse, including the picture — 0.5 pt.
- The cross-sectional area of a horse perpendicular to the sun-rays is 1÷3 arsh² — 0.5 pt.

problems.title: XXI century. Midday.
problems.statement:
As is known, the Republic of Lithuania (see map) uses zone with winter time UT+02 and summer time UT+03. Calculate and draw a conclusion about the following:

![Map of Lithuania with geographic coordinates and towns](#p5-lithuania-astra-s4-r1)

![Equation of time through the year, using the sign convention supplied in the source](#p5-equation-time-astra-s4-r1)

figures.alt: Map of Lithuania with geographic coordinates and towns
Equation of time through the year, using the sign convention supplied in the source

parts.statement: Are there any places in Lithuania, where today (September 8, 2013) the Sun will be exactly in the south at a time when the watches of residents will show just 12:00? (**«да-yes»** or **«нет-no»**).
And in general, on the other days of the year, are there such places? (**«да-yes»** or **«нет-no»**). If "yes", then calculate in what dates, if "no", then justify it by calculations.

solution.statement: Official English solution sketch. The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: 5.1. September 8
sections.statement:
Today (on September 8) the summer time is in operation, so the watches of citizens of Lithuania ahead the universal time by 3 hours. Local mean solar time coincide with this time on the meridian 45° of East longitude, located too far to the east (at the latitude of Lithuania it is in the Nizhny Novgorod region of Russia).

The adding of the equation of time (see figure) is in the range of −16 – +14 minutes, and this effect may replace the meridian not more than 4° in longitude. But even with this addition such areas are far beyond the borders of Lithuania.

Answer: «нет-no».

sections.title: 5.2. Other days of the year
sections.statement:
To answer the second question of the problem you need to consider two periods: summer and winter time. For any of the day during summer time operation the situation is similar to that we discussed in sub-point 1.

The territory of Lithuania is approximately (we can measure it with an accuracy of a quarter degree) between 21°00′ and 26°45′ of East longitude. At the period when the winter time is in operation, the situation is queer. Local mean solar time correspond to the meridian 30° East. Thus, in the winter time period mean local solar noon also does not occur before 12:00 of Lithuanian time anywhere in Lithuania.

However, there is a question about the upper culmination of the sun in the problem condition, as a rule it does not coincide with the mean solar culmination at 12:00 of mean solar time. The difference between the apparent (or true) solar time ($T_A$) and mean solar time ($T_M$) is defined by the equation of time,

$$T_M=T_A+\eta,$$

where $\eta$ is parameter of the equation of time, which is hereinafter referred to as simply “equation of time”, as it is accepted by astronomers.

The meridian 30° East passes very close to the eastern border of Lithuania (about this meridian St. Petersburg, Nevel, Vitebsk, Orsha, Mogilev and Kiev are located), so one should pay attention to the equation of time. Winter time is in operation from the end of October to the end of March, and within this range the values of the equation of time may be both positive and negative.

Positive values of the equation of time move the apparent solar noon to later time (by the watches of inhabitants), and the negative to earlier time. Using the graph of the equation of time one can determine that the adding is minimal on November 3 and its value in a minimum is −16.4 minutes. The corresponding meridian (for the apparent culmination of the Sun at 12:00 Lithuanian time) is shifted by 4°06′ West and by almost a degree enters the territory of Lithuania, till the longitude $\lambda=25^\circ54^{\prime}$.

Thus, the apparent noon will occur at 12:00 of Lithuanian time somewhere at the territory of the country, if the values of the equation of time were below −3°45′ in degrees, and so the values of $\eta$ were below −15 minutes. And $\eta$ is below −15 minutes from October 18 to November 17 (approximately, as we can find from the graph).

Answer: «да-yes», October 18 – November 17 (part of this period when winter time is in operation).

*Note. There is no universally accepted definition of the sign of the equation of time. This solution is written in accordance with the historically European definition of the sign of the equation of time (positive values of $\eta$ in January–March, as it is displayed in the supplement page). However, in the British and American (and also translated from English) literature, the definition is inverse (negative values of $\eta$ in January–March). The members of Jury must consider that solutions using both alternatives of definition are correct (of course, the answer does not depend on the choice of the alternative, turning “+” and “−” at the formula leads to turn the sign of $\eta$ in the equation (1)).*

*Source note: the stated eastern border 26°45′ would differ from 30° by 3°15′, whereas the key subsequently uses 3°45′ and 15 minutes. The printed values and resulting date range are preserved.*

sections.title: Official basic criteria
sections.statement:
**5.1. Totally 3 pt, including:**

- Summer time, meridian 45°, far to the east, so not possible — 2 pt.
- Mention that adding of the equation of time — correction not more than 4° in longitude — 1 pt.

**5.2. Totally 5 pt, including:**

- For any day during summer time the situation is similar #5.1. — 1 pt.
- Finding longitudes of Lithuania, meridian 30° is not too far — 1 pt.
- Correct equation of time using — 1 pt.
- Values of $\eta$ were below −15 minutes — 1 pt.
- Finding the period from October 18 to November 17 (approximately) — 1 pt.

problems.title: Supernova remnant
problems.statement:
An X-ray image of supernova remnant (SNR) Cas A located at a distance of d = 3400 pc was obtained using Chandra Space Observatory. The negative of this image is shown in Fig. SNR. The boundaries of the SNR region are marked by a circle. The scale of the image is shown in the upper left corner of the figure. A dot located close to the center of the circle is the neutron star – the remaining core of the collapsed star. The rectangular marks outside the circle are given for the reference when determining the center of the circle.

Assume that the amount of energy released in the supernova explosion was about $E_{\mathrm{SN}} \approx 10^{46}\ \mathrm{J}$, 1% of which drives the expansion of the remnant. The average density of the matter in the SNR is $\rho \approx 10^{-21}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

![SNR Cas A: 100 arcsecond scale, boundary circle and external reference marks](#p6-snr-astra-s4-r1)

figures.alt: SNR Cas A: 100 arcsecond scale, boundary circle and external reference marks

parts.statement: Estimate the age of the SNR Cas A.
Calculate the average velocity of the motion of the neutron star from the center of the SNR.

solution.statement: Official English solution sketch. The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: 6.1. Age of the supernova remnant
sections.statement:
Assume that the SNR is a sphere with the linear radius R. Using a ruler we accurately measure the diameter of the circle and the scale length (e.g. in mm) in Fig. SNR (see the figure below, the initial figure was almost 2 times larger). From the measurements we get the radius of the circle $\rho=48.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ and 100″ scale length $l=28.5\ \mathrm{mm}$. With these data we can calculate the angular radius of the SNR

$$\theta=100^{\prime\prime}\rho/l,$$

$$\theta=100^{\prime\prime}\times48.5/28.5\approx170^{\prime\prime}.$$

If the radius R of the SNR is measured in au, the distance d in pc, and its angular radius $\theta$ in arcsec, then

$$R=d\times\theta,$$

$$R=170^{\prime\prime}\times3400=578000\ \mathrm{AU}\approx8.6\cdot10^{16}\ \mathrm m.$$

The mass of the SNR is confined within the sphere of the radius R.

$$M=\rho\cdot\frac43\pi R^3,$$

$$M=10^{-21}\cdot4/3\cdot3.14\cdot(8.5\cdot10^{16})^3\approx2.7\cdot10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}.$$

The expansion speed of the SNR is calculated using the expression of the kinetic energy of the SNR

$$E_{\mathrm{kin}}=\tfrac12Mv^2,$$

$$v=(2E_{\mathrm{kin}}/M)^{1/2}=(2\cdot0.01E_{\mathrm{SN}}/M)^{1/2},$$

$$v=(2\cdot0.01\cdot10^{46}\ \mathrm J/(2.7\cdot10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}))^{1/2}\approx8.6\cdot10^6\ \mathrm{m/s}\approx10^7\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$

As we see from the image, the darkest parts of it are distributed at distances about 60% of its radius. So we may propose that most mass of the SNR is distributed at these distances. Thus, by the above formulae we have found the average speed of matter at 0.6 R.

Assuming that the expansion velocity was constant we get the age of the SNR:

$$t=0.6R/v,$$

$$t=0.6\times8.6\cdot10^{16}\ \mathrm m/(8.6\cdot10^6\ \mathrm{m/s})\approx6\cdot10^9\ \mathrm s\approx190\ \mathrm{yr}\approx200\ \mathrm{yr}.$$

Taking into account that most data in the problem conditions was given very roughly, with maximum 1 significant digit (and even with zero significant digits as only order of magnitude is done: the energy was about $10^{46}$ J, 1% of which drives the expansion; the average density is $10^{-21}$ kg/m³), the answer should be expressed with only one significant digit.

So the answer is: ~200 years.

*Source note: the key uses $\rho$ both for the measured image radius and for the matter density, and uses $8.5\cdot10^{16}$ m in the mass calculation after $8.6\cdot10^{16}$ m above. These are retained.*

![Cas A image with reference circle and measurement lines in the official solution](#p6-measured-snr-astra-s4-r1)

figures.alt: Cas A image with reference circle and measurement lines in the official solution

sections.title: 6.2. Neutron-star velocity
sections.statement:
Using a ruler we measure the distance of the neutron star from the center of circle in Fig. SNR. Say that we get $\sigma=3\ \mathrm{mm}$. Then the angular distance of the neutron star from the center of the SNR is

$$\delta=100^{\prime\prime}\sigma/l,$$

$$\delta=100^{\prime\prime}\times3/28.5\approx10.5^{\prime\prime}.$$

The linear distance of the neutron star from the center of the SNR is

$$S_N=\sigma\times d,$$

$$S_N=10.5\times3400\approx35700\ \mathrm{AU}\approx5.3\cdot10^{12}\ \mathrm{km}.$$

The velocity of the motion of the neutron star is

$$u=S_N/t,$$

$$u=5.3\cdot10^{12}\ \mathrm{km}/(6\cdot10^9\ \mathrm s)\approx900\ \mathrm{km/s}\approx10^3\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

Also taking into account that most data was done very roughly, the answer should be expressed also as an order of magnitude only or with only one significant digit.

The answer is: ~$10^3$ km/s.

*Source note: the key prints $S_N=\sigma d$ although the substituted 10.5 is the angular distance $\delta$; its notation is preserved.*

sections.title: Official basic criteria
sections.statement:
**6.1. Totally 4 pt, including:**

- Correct measurements of distances — 0.5 pt.
- Finding necessary distances and mass — 1.5 pt.
- Energy, finding typical speeds — 1 pt.
- Find the time, correct calculations — 1 pt.

**6.2. Totally 2 pt, including:**

- Correct measurements of distance from the center — 0.5 pt.
- Calculations and correct answer — 1.5 pt.

**6.common. Totally 2 pt, including:**

- The most data in the problem conditions was given very roughly, with maximum 1 significant digit, so the answer should be expressed with only one significant digit, follow this principle — 2 pt.
